paper.authors_full: Peidong Mei, Deborah N. Brewis, Fortune Nwaiwu, Deshan Sumanathilaka, Fernando Alva-Manchego, Joanna Demaree-Cotton
paper.title: If ChatGPT can do it, where is my creativity? generative AI boosts performance but diminishes experience in creative writing
paper.venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
paper.pdf_filename: Mei et al (2025) - If ChatGPT can do it, where is my creativity.pdf
paper.version_read: Journal version of record, Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 4 (2025), article 100140; accepted and available online 19 March 2025 (PDF p. 1).
paper.one_line_finding: In an online experiment that randomly assigned UK university students to use or not use ChatGPT on a 10-minute task listing uses for a 'printer that can print anything in 2097' (225 analyzed), the AI arm's mean counts of uses and of conceptual domains were above Control's in all four subgroups (Fig. 2, p. 6), with no significant difference in frequency in Group 2 (b = 0.91, SE = 2.30, p = .69) or on either count in Group 4 (p. 6), and the AI condition's pooled outputs scored higher on group-level frequency (635 vs 552) and flexibility (442 vs 313) (Fig. 5, p. 9); pooled regressions are only in SI Table 3, not in this PDF.

studies.label: Online experiment: printer-uses writing task with vs without ChatGPT

counts_source.quote: Forty-three people who failed the attention check were excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 225.

arms.name: AI
arms.description: Randomly assigned participants were explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task; they reported their usage after the task (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2).

studies.task: Write approximately 100 words in 10 minutes describing as many unique uses as possible for a hypothetical printer that can print anything in 2097, while minimizing grammatical errors and maximizing clarity (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2).

estimates.notes: The treatment_mean and control_mean fields contain arm-level set counts, not participant averages; no averaging or difference calculation was performed. Numbers are transcribed from the prose on PDF p. 7 and assigned to the outcome using the bottom frequency panel of Fig. 5 on PDF p. 9, matching the reconciled screening form. The prose swaps the frequency/flexibility labels. Fig. 5's caption also reverses the use/nonuse wording; treatment assignment follows the figure's explicit AI/Control legend, checked visually. These numbers also appear in the prose and were not inferred from bar heights. Higher counts are interpreted by the paper as greater collective diversity (PDF p. 10, Section 4.2.3), although the calculation is underdescribed. No uncertainty, per-arm participant counts, or explicit count of participants contributing to this pooled outcome is printed. The observation is each condition’s full set of outputs; n_units remains null because no observation count is printed. SI Table 5 was unavailable.

estimates.primary_override_reason: across_people, ai_vs_bau. Neither group-level count is a semantic-similarity measure. The count of distinct conceptual domains across each arm's pool measures how varied the ideas are across people; the count of different uses tracks the number of ideas. Same choice as the paper's with_ai record (flexibility over fluency).

open_items: SI Tables 1-6 are cited but absent from the supplied PDF, which has no embedded attachments; the c161 entry in supplement-manifest.json lists no files. No separate supplement was located beside the PDF. During reconciliation, urllib requests to the named DOI, Oxford repository record, and OSF registration API all failed with a local socket-permission error (WinError 10013). No supplement or registration was inspected.

SI Table 3 is needed to verify full-sample frequency, flexibility, inaccuracy, and unclarity coefficients, SEs, p-values, model specification, and analysis counts. The main PDF prints only subgroup coefficients for these individual outcomes and no full-sample numerical arm means or SDs (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 3.1-3.2).

Total randomized count, AI and Control arm sizes, and outcome-specific contributing participant counts are not printed. The stated final sample of 225 is retained at study level only; estimate-level counts are null (PDF p. 4, Section 2.1).

Participant accounting is internally inconsistent: the paper states 266 completions, forty-three exclusions, and a final sample of 225. The total has not been repaired by arithmetic. The perception-test degrees of freedom on PDF p. 8 are not printed participant counts and were not used to infer any count.
The position of the attention check and whether assignment was stratified by English proficiency and prior ChatGPT experience are not stated (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 2.1-2.2).

For the group-level counts, the treatment of duplicate ideas, domain aggregation, normalization by arm size, contributing participant counts, and uncertainty are not described. SI Table 5 may clarify them (PDF p. 7, Section 3.2.3).

The full-sample labels in the PDF p. 7 prose conflict with Fig. 5: the prose calls 635 versus 552 flexibility and 442 versus 313 frequency. The retained outcome assignments follow the independently checked figure panel labels and legend on PDF p. 9. The figure caption also reverses the use/nonuse wording. Both publication inconsistencies remain documented.

The participant-facing ChatGPT model, tier, access route, and detailed usage instructions are unspecified. The recorded year is the product release year printed in the introduction, not an inferred model year (PDF pp. 1 and 5).
The paper names GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo for automatic scoring without identifying which model supplied the analyzed counts (PDF p. 5, Section 2.3).

The article states that the study was preregistered, but it does not identify a specific preregistered primary outcome; the linked registration could not be inspected (PDF p. 4, Section 2.1; PDF pp. 12-13, Pre-registration).
